metadata.title: The effect of compulsory education on non-cognitive skills: Evidence from low- and middle-income countries

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses World Bank STEP household survey data (urban residents aged 15–64) for Bolivia, Colombia, Ghana, and Vietnam, and constructs treatment/control groups using birth-cohort cutoffs tied to compulsory schooling reforms. The analytic samples are restricted to individuals older than 23 and to specific birth-year windows (3-, 5-, and 10-year samples) around each reform cutoff; standard errors are clustered on the reform × birth-year level. The manuscript does not report applying STEP sampling weights or any replicate-weight scheme, and it does not name a weight variable (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT). Because the empirical strategy is a quasi-experimental regression discontinuity–style cohort design with clustered standard errors, the paper’s inference relies on the reported clustering rather than explicit complex-survey weighting.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in the main results are non-cognitive skill measures (Big Five short-form personality traits, grit, hostile attribution bias, decision-making patterns, and binary risk/patience indicators) derived from STEP questionnaire items and hypothetical choices; these are not PISA/TIMSS-style cognitive achievement plausible values. The paper does not describe a missing-data strategy for these measures (e.g., listwise deletion, imputation), so the handling of missing questionnaire responses is a reporting gap. While the appendix provides sample sizes for the restricted birth-window samples, it does not specify how missing skill items were treated.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses World Bank STEP household survey data for urban residents aged 15–64 in Bolivia, Colombia, Ghana, and Vietnam (Philippines excluded for comparability). Treatment is defined by birth year relative to each reform’s pivotal cohort cutoff; individuals born in the pivotal cohort year or later are treated, those born before are controls. The estimation sample is further restricted to individuals older than 23 to ensure treated individuals have likely completed advanced education. Main results use birth-year windows of 5 years (preferred), plus robustness using 3-year and 10-year windows, where the window includes individuals born within x years before or after the cohort cutoff. The paper also reports a balanced-sample check and controls for number of siblings at age 12 when estimating the main specification.

main_findings.dataset_used: STEP household survey (2012/2013), urban residents aged 15–64; compulsory schooling reforms (Bolivia 1994, Colombia 1991, Ghana 1961 & 1987, Vietnam 1991); 5-year birth-window; non-cognitive skills (personality traits & behaviors)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Preferred specification (5-year sample, linear cohort trends): ATE = −0.23 SD (SE 0.08), p<0.01 (Table 5, column (1)).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using STEP household survey data from Bolivia, Colombia, Ghana, and Vietnam around compulsory schooling reform cohort cutoffs, the study leveraged gender, SES at age 15, parental involvement, and siblings at age 12 (as controls in the balanced specification) to estimate the effect on emotional stability, finding that compulsory education reforms decreased emotional stability by 0.23 standard deviations. This indicates that extending mandatory schooling can shift personality-related emotional stability in ways that may require attention in education policy and student support, though the design is quasi-experimental and does not identify mechanisms.

main_findings.dataset_used: STEP household survey (2012/2013), urban residents aged 15–64; compulsory schooling reforms (Bolivia 1994, Colombia 1991, Ghana 1961 & 1987, Vietnam 1991); 5-year birth-window; non-cognitive skills (personality traits & behaviors)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Preferred specification (5-year sample, linear cohort trends): ATE = +0.14 SD (SE 0.06), p<0.05 (Table 5, column (1)).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using STEP household survey data from Bolivia, Colombia, Ghana, and Vietnam around compulsory schooling reform cohort cutoffs, the study leveraged gender, SES at age 15, parental involvement, and siblings at age 12 (as controls in the balanced specification) to estimate the effect on openness to experience, finding that compulsory education reforms increased openness to experience by 0.14 standard deviations. This indicates that education policy that increases years of compulsory schooling may foster openness-related traits that are potentially valuable for adaptability, while causality is limited to effects near cohort cutoffs.

main_findings.dataset_used: STEP household survey (2012/2013), urban residents aged 15–64; compulsory schooling reforms (Bolivia 1994, Colombia 1991, Ghana 1961 & 1987, Vietnam 1991); 5-year birth-window; non-cognitive skills (personality traits & behaviors)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Preferred specification (5-year sample, linear cohort trends): ATE = +0.10 SD (SE 0.05), p<0.1 (Table 5, column (1)).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using STEP household survey data from Bolivia, Colombia, Ghana, and Vietnam around compulsory schooling reform cohort cutoffs, the study leveraged gender, SES at age 15, parental involvement, and siblings at age 12 (as controls in the balanced specification) to estimate the effect on decision-making patterns, finding that compulsory education reforms improved decision-making patterns by 0.10 standard deviations. This indicates that education policy may strengthen students’ alternative-solution and consequential-thinking behaviors, though the effect size is modest and inference is local to cohort cutoffs.

main_findings.dataset_used: STEP household survey (2012/2013), urban residents aged 15–64; compulsory schooling reforms (Bolivia 1994, Colombia 1991, Ghana 1961 & 1987, Vietnam 1991); 5-year birth-window; non-cognitive skills (personality traits & behaviors)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Preferred specification (5-year sample, linear cohort trends): ATE = −0.14 SD (SE 0.06), p<0.05 (Table 5, column (1)).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using STEP household survey data from Bolivia, Colombia, Ghana, and Vietnam around compulsory schooling reform cohort cutoffs, the study leveraged gender, SES at age 15, parental involvement, and siblings at age 12 (as controls in the balanced specification) to estimate the effect on grit, finding that compulsory education reforms reduced grit by 0.14 standard deviations. This indicates that simply increasing compulsory years may not uniformly build perseverance traits and may even lower them, suggesting that education policy should pair expansion with supportive learning environments that sustain long-term goal commitment.

main_findings.dataset_used: STEP household survey (2012/2013), urban residents aged 15–64; compulsory schooling reforms (Bolivia 1994, Colombia 1991, Ghana 1961 & 1987, Vietnam 1991); 5-year birth-window; non-cognitive skills (personality traits & behaviors)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Preferred specification (5-year sample, linear cohort trends): ATE = −0.21 SD (SE 0.06), p<0.01 (Table 5, column (1)).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using STEP household survey data from Bolivia, Colombia, Ghana, and Vietnam around compulsory schooling reform cohort cutoffs, the study leveraged gender, SES at age 15, parental involvement, and siblings at age 12 (as controls in the balanced specification) to estimate the effect on hostile attribution bias, finding that compulsory education reforms decreased hostile attribution bias by 0.21 standard deviations. This indicates that education policy that increases compulsory schooling can reduce a risk-related social-cognition bias, potentially improving social interactions and downstream labor-market productivity, though the study does not establish the specific mechanism.

main_findings.dataset_used: STEP household survey (2012/2013), urban residents aged 15–64; compulsory schooling reforms (Bolivia 1994, Colombia 1991, Ghana 1961 & 1987, Vietnam 1991); 5-year birth-window; non-cognitive skills (preferences)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Preferred specification (5-year sample, linear cohort trends): ATE = −0.06 (SE 0.02), p<0.01 (Table 6, column (1)); interpreted as −6% probability patient.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using STEP household survey data from Bolivia, Colombia, Ghana, and Vietnam around compulsory schooling reform cohort cutoffs, the study leveraged gender, SES at age 15, parental involvement, and siblings at age 12 (as controls in the balanced specification) to estimate the effect on patience, finding that compulsory education reforms reduced the probability of being patient by 6%. This indicates that education expansion may lower patience in these low- and middle-income contexts, implying that policy should consider context-dependent effects and potentially improve education quality and perceived value to avoid reducing time-horizon preferences.

main_findings.dataset_used: STEP household survey (2012/2013), urban residents aged 15–64; compulsory schooling reforms (Bolivia 1994, Colombia 1991, Ghana 1961 & 1987, Vietnam 1991); 5-year birth-window; non-cognitive skills (preferences)
main_findings.target_variable: Willingness to take risk (binary; probability risk-taking)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Preferred specification (5-year sample, linear cohort trends): ATE = −0.05 (SE 0.03), p<0.1 (Table 6, column (1)); interpreted as −5% probability willing to take risk.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using STEP household survey data from Bolivia, Colombia, Ghana, and Vietnam around compulsory schooling reform cohort cutoffs, the study leveraged gender, SES at age 15, parental involvement, and siblings at age 12 (as controls in the balanced specification) to estimate the effect on willingness to take risk, finding that compulsory education reforms reduced the probability of taking risks by 5%. This indicates that education policy that increases compulsory years can shift economic preferences toward lower risk-taking, which may affect productivity and earnings depending on labor-market demands, while the effect is estimated locally around cohort cutoffs.

data.outcome_summary: The paper estimates causal effects of compulsory schooling reforms on non-cognitive skills using World Bank STEP household survey data from Bolivia, Colombia, Ghana, and Vietnam (urban residents aged 15–64), exploiting within-country birth-cohort cutoffs tied to reforms. The preferred specification uses a 5-year birth window around each pivotal cohort and linear cohort trends, with standard errors clustered on reform × birth-year; the study does not use machine learning models. Across the five reforms, compulsory education increases openness to experience (+0.14 SD) and decision-making patterns (+0.10 SD) and decreases emotional stability (−0.23 SD), grit (−0.14 SD), hostile attribution bias (−0.21 SD), patience (−0.06; about −6% probability), and willingness to take risks (−0.05; about −5% probability). The paper further links these skill changes to wages via augmented Mincer wage regressions, predicting an overall wage increase of 9%, with about 40% of the predicted increase attributed to non-cognitive skill changes. Limitations include short Big Five item sets, single cross-sectional measurement, and no reported missing-data strategy or survey-weight application.
